QuestionExcerpt: Please may you expand on the very last point you made: if power is flowing from hot through the ground, and it's very low (think you said current because high resistance?) What would happen in this case? It won't trip the breaker, so will keep flowing indefinitely? Or will it cause other issues in the home? I'd get a shock too (more like a tingle) if I was to touch the bare earth under this fault condition? Thanks!
QuestionSummary: What are the electrical consequences if a hot conductor faults to earth with high resistance (low fault current): will overcurrent protection trip, will current persist, what hazards in the dwelling and is there risk of step/touch shock?
AnswerExcerpt: so it won't trip the breaker or anything else, and will just sit there heating the ground up around the rod.
AnswerSummary: An isolated hot-to-ground fault into a single earth electrode typically produces only a few amps due to earth electrode resistance, so overcurrent devices usually won't operate; however the electrode and nearby ground can become energized, producing hazardous step/touch potentials and local heating. Conversely, if the earth electrode is bonded into the neutral/ground system the fault current will be large and should trip protective devices.
ReplySummary: Replies state that if the ground electrode is bonded to the neutral/service, a hot-to-ground fault produces high fault current that trips overcurrent protection; if the rod is isolated the earth path yields only a few amps so breakers may not trip, but the rod can be energized and create dangerous step/touch voltages and local heating. NEC bonding and ground rod resistance (25 Ω requirement, 8 ft rod) and voltage‑gradient hazards are cited.

QuestionExcerpt: Since this is AC, wouldn't the hot and neutral wire switch continuously as the electrons reverse?  Therefore why bother to distinguish between them?
QuestionSummary: Asks whether electron reversal in AC causes hot and neutral to swap roles and why the conductors are distinguished.
AnswerExcerpt: Current flows *through* the circuit, and so yes, the 'neutral' has just as much current as the 'hot.'
AnswerSummary: The neutral conducts the alternating current just like the hot; the distinction is that the neutral is the grounded conductor clamped to earth potential to define voltage reference and provide a fault return. Disconnecting the neutral (open neutral) removes that reference and can make the conductor hazardous.
ReplySummary: Respondents agree that although instantaneous current polarity reverses, the ungrounded conductor (hot) supplies the alternating voltage while the grounded conductor (neutral) provides the defined low-impedance return and reference to earth. Replies clarify voltage is a potential between conductors, neutral carries current (or the difference between split-phase legs), and an open neutral creates hazardous conditions.

QuestionExcerpt: I still don't know what a "short" is, because the neutral is connected to the hot in the transformer. This is called a "short" if you watch any other explanation of a "short." Why does a short create a dangerous condition elsewhere when it does not cause danger in the transformer?
QuestionSummary: Asks why a "short" (hot-to-neutral connection) is dangerous externally even though the transformer ties neutral to hot at its winding, and what defines a short.
AnswerExcerpt: A short-circuit is a circuit path of little resistance from the source and back to the source.
AnswerSummary: The best reply states that a short-circuit is a low-resistance path directly returning to the source. Because a transformer and its windings have finite impedance, internal connections don't produce massive current, but external low-impedance faults do, causing high fault current, overheating, and tripping of overcurrent protection.
ReplySummary: Replies define a short-circuit as a low-impedance path that diverts current from the intended load. Respondents note transformer winding impedance/reactance limits internal current, while external low-impedance faults produce large fault currents that can overheat conductors, cause electrocution if a person becomes the path, and are detected by overcurrent devices.

QuestionExcerpt: Why does water trip circuits even if it is only in contact with a live wire only or a neutral wire only?
QuestionSummary: Asks why conductive water contacting either a line (hot) conductor or a neutral conductor can cause circuit breakers to trip.
AnswerExcerpt: If the water is touching ground or anything connected to ground, then there will be a voltage between the water and the live wire
AnswerSummary: When water provides a conductive path between a live conductor and earth/ground-referenced objects, a high fault current flows and trips overcurrent protection. An open or disconnected neutral can become energized, so water contact may also cause current in that case; contact with a bonded neutral at near-earth potential usually does not.
ReplySummary: Reply explains that water contacting ground-referenced objects creates a voltage difference with a live conductor, causing large fault current and tripping protection; an open/disconnected neutral can become energized, while contact with a solid neutral typically produces no voltage difference.

AnswerExcerpt: The RMS was originally found by finding the equivalent of the DC load.
AnswerSummary: RMS is defined so an AC waveform delivers the same average power (heating) to a resistive load as a DC value; squaring prevents positive/negative cancellation and averaging then square-rooting yields the RMS. Multimeters implement this formula—cheap units estimate, while true-RMS instruments compute the correct value.

QuestionSummary: Clarification requested on conductor role in AC: why one conductor is labelled 'hot' while the return is 'neutral', and why a voltage tester detects hot but not neutral.
AnswerExcerpt: Because the neutral is grounded and so are you. There is no difference in voltage between these points, only before the load

IF electricity takes ALL paths back to ground, not just the path of least resistance AND the neutral bus bar is carrying say 5 amps, since it is bonded to the ground bus bar, how come we don't have some of that current flowing through the ground as well?

AnswerExcerpt: There is no flow because the ground is connected to the "case" not the operational load.
AnswerSummary: The grounding conductor/E GC is an equipment safety conductor, not a normal current-carrying neutral; it only conducts during faults. QuestionExcerpt: What happens if two live wires touch with each other? well, i know, the breaker pops, but why? and what are the dangers in that?
QuestionSummary: Asks what occurs when two hot conductors contact, why the circuit breaker trips, and the associated hazards such as fault current and equipment damage.
AnswerExcerpt: a current will flow from the higher to the lower voltage level source
AnswerSummary: If the two hots are at the same potential (same source/phase) little or no current flows; if they are at different potentials a line-to-line short occurs, producing large fault current that trips overcurrent protection and can cause arcing, conductor heating, and equipment damage.
ReplySummary: Reply states the outcome depends on whether the conductors share the same source/phase; if they are at different potentials a current flows from higher to lower potential, creating a high-current independent circuit that can damage connected loads and trip protection. Kirchhoff's laws are cited as the governing principle.

QuestionExcerpt: So if you touch the washing machine metal casing that has current returning through the ground wire instead of neutral will you feel any shock/small tingle or is our resistance too high compared to the casing?  Thanks in advance.
QuestionSummary: Asks whether contacting a washing machine chassis carrying fault current on the equipment grounding conductor (EGC) instead of the neutral will produce a perceptible shock given human body versus chassis/EGC impedance.
AnswerExcerpt: That completes a low-resistance circuit, allowing much current to flow, quickly tripping the breaker or blowing the fuse.
AnswerSummary: Bonding the metal chassis to the equipment grounding conductor establishes a low-impedance fault path back to the service neutral at the main bonding jumper, producing sufficient fault current to trip the breaker. ReplySummary: Replies concur that a properly bonded equipment grounding conductor provides a low-impedance return that should prevent a perceptible shock by creating high fault current to trip overcurrent protection. What would cause a hot wire to just randomly touch a metal casing?
